title: Active and passive contributions to spatial learning
review_question: How does the mode of exploration (active vs. passive) in a new environment influence the resulting spatial knowledge (landmark, route, and survey knowledge)?
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Not explicitly stated, but focuses on studies comparing active and passive spatial learning, primarily using virtual reality (desktop and ambulatory) and real-world environments.

findings.antecedent: Idiothetic information (motor, proprioceptive, vestibular) during walking
findings.quote: idiothetic information contributes to spatial updating in small-scale environments, to path integration in large-scale environments, and to spatial learning of survey knowledge.

findings.antecedent: Idiothetic information (motor, proprioceptive)
findings.quote: There is preliminary evidence that motor and proprioceptive information also contribute to route knowledge, perhaps by better specifying the action (turn angle and distance) in each place-action association.

findings.antecedent: Decision making during exploration (without idiothetic information, e.g., desktop VR)
findings.quote: there is little evidence that making decisions about one's path during exploration, in the absence of idiothetic information, contributes to spatial learning.

findings.antecedent: Decision making about exploratory behavior
findings.consequent: Route knowledge (in children) and other types of spatial memory
findings.source: Conclusions: Idiothetic information, decision making, and attention
findings.quote: Hazen reported better route finding by children who had freely explored than by those who were led by their parents, suggesting a role for decision making in route knowledge.

findings.antecedent: Allocation of attention to relevant environmental properties
findings.consequent: Acquisition of route and survey knowledge
findings.quote: the allocation of attention to relevant environmental properties clearly contributes to the acquisition of route and survey knowledge.

findings.antecedent: Incidental encoding (without explicit attention)
findings.consequent: Landmarks, landmark-boundary relations, and sequences of landmarks
findings.quote: Whereas landmarks, their relation to boundaries, and possibly landmark sequences appear to be encoded incidentally, landmark-action associations and spatial relations among landmarks require the intention to learn, implicating attention.

findings.antecedent: Intentional encoding (with explicit attention)
findings.consequent: Landmark-action associations and spatial relations among landmarks
findings.quote: In contrast, the selection of informative landmarks, place-action associations, and spatial relations among landmarks appears to depend on tasks that direct active attention to the corresponding environmental properties.

findings.antecedent: Directing attention to place-action associations
findings.quote: Directing attention to place-action associations facilitates route learning at the expense of survey learning...

findings.antecedent: Directing attention to configural relations
findings.quote: ...whereas directing attention to configural relations facilitates survey knowledge but may not impact route knowledge.

findings.antecedent: Absence of idiothetic information (e.g., desktop VR)
findings.consequent: Influence of attention on survey learning
findings.quote: The absence of idiothetic information in desktop VR may have masked the contribution of attention, making the presence of idiothetic information necessary to test the contribution of attention to the acquisition of survey knowledge.

findings.antecedent: Verbal working memory
findings.consequent: Encoding of route information (from text, slides, passive VR, walking)
findings.quote: verbal working memory seems to play a role in encoding route information, whether it is presented via text, slide sequences, passive VR, or walking with idiothetic information.

findings.antecedent: Spatial-sequential working memory
findings.consequent: Encoding of route knowledge (from text and VR displays)
findings.quote: spatial-sequential working memory also appears to contribute to the encoding of route knowledge from both text and VR displays.

findings.antecedent: Spatial-simultaneous working memory
findings.consequent: Encoding of survey knowledge (from visual maps)
findings.quote: spatial-simultaneous working memory is implicated in the encoding of survey knowledge from visual maps...

findings.antecedent: Active mental manipulation of spatial information in working memory
findings.quote: active manipulation of spatial information in working memory may enhance spatial learning.

findings.antecedent: Active exploration (walking with idiothetic information)
findings.consequent: Spatial learning (place, landmark, route, and/or survey knowledge)
findings.quote: In sum, there appears to be a reliable active advantage in spatial learning, such that it is task dependent.

findings.antecedent: Physical movement (vs. imagined movement)
findings.consequent: Spatial updating (faster and more accurate pointing estimates)
findings.quote: pointing estimates from a novel location are faster and more accurate when participants physically move to that location than when they just imagine moving to it

findings.antecedent: Motor and/or proprioceptive information (e.g., joystick control of rotation)
findings.quote: it appears having some measure of control over when the rotations start and stop, without deciding how far to turn, improves the accuracy of spatial updating.

findings.antecedent: Vestibular and proprioceptive information (self-motion)
findings.quote: the addition of vestibular and proprioceptive information in the self-motion condition led to shorter response times and fewer errors, as compared with visual and motor information alone in the display motion condition.

findings.antecedent: Rich visual scene (including landmarks) in a well-known environment
findings.quote: the full scene including landmarks was sufficient for automatic and obligatory spatial updating, even without a physical rotation.

findings.antecedent: Active movement around a display
findings.quote: Wang and Simons effectively demonstrated that spatial updating can occur when one actively moves around a display

findings.antecedent: Motor and proprioceptive information
findings.consequent: Learning routes and some survey knowledge
findings.quote: These two studies indicate that motor and proprioceptive information are vital to learning routes, as well as to some survey knowledge, while rotational information contributes minimally to wayfinding.

findings.antecedent: Physical turns (vs. joystick turns)
findings.consequent: Learning (reduced total distance traveled during search)
findings.quote: They found that the addition of physical translation aided learning only by leading to less total distance traveled during search.

findings.antecedent: Walking (vs. physical rotation/joystick for translation/rotation)
findings.consequent: Performance in searching for hidden objects
findings.quote: They found better performance for those who walked, as compared with those who physically rotated but translated with a joystick and those who used a joystick for both rotation and translation.

findings.antecedent: Active exploration (vs. passive viewing) in desktop VR
findings.source: Motor control and decision making in desktop VR
findings.quote: However, there was no difference between the active and passive groups: Both showed higher accuracy and faster reaction times for familiar views than for novel views of the same environment.

findings.antecedent: Continuous visual motion during exploration (vs. snapshots)
findings.source: Motor control and decision making in desktop VR
findings.quote: When passive observers viewed only snapshots of the display, performance on novel views dropped dramatically, to the level of mirror-reversed views. This result confirms an advantage of continuous visual motion during exploration of the environment.

findings.antecedent: Active exploration (vs. passive viewing) in desktop VR
findings.source: Motor control and decision making in desktop VR
findings.quote: Any effects of active versus passive exploration in desktop VR are small and unreliable and may be susceptible to minor procedural differences.

findings.antecedent: Active exploration (joystick) with attention to objects (vs. passive viewing)
findings.source: Attention to spatial and nonspatial properties
findings.quote: Active participants explored the environment using a joystick and performed better on subsequent recall tests of spatial layout than did passive participants who viewed a corresponding display.

findings.antecedent: Passive viewing with attention to objects
findings.source: Attention to spatial and nonspatial properties
findings.quote: when they attend to objects, their layout learning suffers.

findings.antecedent: Intentional learning of a route
findings.consequent: Route knowledge (map filling, reverse route errors)
findings.source: Incidental and intentional learning of spatial information
findings.quote: The intentional-encoding group more accurately filled in the route on a map of the building and made fewer errors when reversing the route on foot than did the incidental-encoding group.

findings.antecedent: Intentional learning of an object array (vs. incidental learning) in children
findings.source: Incidental and intentional learning of spatial information
findings.quote: In children, intentional learning of an object array proves to be no better than incidental learning, suggesting that spatial information may be acquired with little effort.

findings.antecedent: Intentional learning of layout (vs. incidental learning) when reproducing objects on a table
findings.source: Incidental and intentional learning of spatial information
findings.quote: intentional learning appears to improve performance when the task is to reproduce the layout by placing the objects on a table immediately after viewing

findings.antecedent: Intentional learning of layout (vs. incidental learning) with delayed reproduction task
findings.source: Incidental and intentional learning of spatial information
findings.quote: When the reproduction task is delayed for several minutes, the performance of the incidental group suffers, while the intentional group remains fairly accurate.

findings.antecedent: Tasks emphasizing learning relationship between objects and a landmark
findings.source: Incidental and intentional learning of spatial information
findings.quote: blocking when people performed tasks that emphasized learning the relationship between objects and a landmark

findings.antecedent: Tasks emphasizing learning relationship between objects and an environmental boundary
findings.source: Incidental and intentional learning of spatial information
findings.quote: ...but not when the tasks emphasized learning the relationship between objects and an environmental boundary.

findings.antecedent: Intentional processing of relations among features
findings.source: Incidental and intentional learning of spatial information
findings.quote: intentional processing of those relations among features leads to greater spatial learning.

findings.antecedent: Daily task of following known routes
findings.quote: nurses who worked in a complex hospital building did not acquire survey knowledge of the building even after 2 years of experience.

findings.antecedent: Learning by studying a map (vs. walking in environment)
findings.quote: participants who learned the building by studying a map tended to show an advantage on both route and survey tests over those who learned it by walking in the environment

findings.antecedent: Older adults' attention
findings.consequent: Selection of informative landmarks for navigation
findings.quote: Rather than paying attention to landmarks that are relevant to finding the route, they appear to attend to those that are most perceptually salient.

findings.antecedent: Children's attention
findings.consequent: Selection of informative landmarks for navigation
findings.quote: children tend to select highly noticeable but spatially uninformative landmarks

findings.antecedent: Verbal information about landmarks at decision points
findings.quote: Verbal information about landmarks at decision points has proven to be most informative when a route is followed

synthesis_conclusions: Idiothetic information from walking is crucial for acquiring metric survey knowledge and contributes to route knowledge.
The influence of decision-making on spatial learning is weak and unreliable, especially in desktop VR, but may play a role in route knowledge for children and other spatial memory types.

Attention to relevant environmental properties significantly contributes to route and survey knowledge, with landmarks and boundaries learned incidentally, but place-action associations and landmark relations requiring intentional attention.
Verbal and spatial-sequential working memory are involved in encoding route information, while spatial-simultaneous working memory is implicated in map-based survey knowledge.
Active mental manipulation of spatial information in working memory may enhance spatial learning.
There is a reliable active advantage in spatial learning, which is task-dependent and allows humans to modulate learning based on goals and environmental properties.
evidence_gaps: Lack of research investigating the contribution of idiothetic information, decision making, and spatial attention in the same experimental paradigm, especially regarding route knowledge.
Unexamined possible additive effects or interactions between idiothetic information, decision making, and spatial attention.
Need for further studies in ambulatory environments to investigate decision making and spatial attention's contribution to spatial learning when normal idiothetic information is available.
The hypothesis that decision making is sufficient for route learning remains to be tested.
The relationship between working memory components and the acquisition of survey knowledge is largely unknown, beyond map-based learning.
Need for more work with immersive spatial learning to confirm the role of mental manipulation.
The underlying neural bases of active and passive spatial learning are relatively unexplored, especially in humans due to neuroimaging limitations with physical movement.
heterogeneity_sources: Inconsistent methods across studies (e.g., desktop VR vs. ambulatory VR vs. real-world)
Differences in motor and proprioceptive information provided by different VR setups (joystick vs. keyboard vs. walking in place)
Lack of decision making during exploration in some 'active' conditions
Failure to equate visual input or routes of exploration between active and passive groups
Variations in environment size and visibility (small object arrays vs. room/building/campus-sized)
Use of different measures of spatial knowledge (layout recall vs. pointing/distance estimates)
Confounding of attention allocation with active/passive conditions

moderators.effect: Idiothetic information's effect on spatial learning is more pronounced with sufficiently complex paths or after repeated exposure to the environment.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Passive vision may be sufficient for simple environments, but idiothetic learning builds up over time for complex ones.

moderators.effect: Older adults require motor and proprioceptive information for path integration, whereas vestibular information alone is sufficient for young adults.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Older adults also have difficulty with route retracing, landmark ordering, and selecting informative landmarks, tending to focus on perceptually salient ones.

moderators.effect: The type of spatial knowledge acquired (landmark, route, survey) depends on the specific task demands and how attention is directed during learning.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Directing attention to place-action associations facilitates route learning at the expense of survey learning, while attention to configural relations facilitates survey knowledge.

moderators.effect: Active simultaneous working memory tasks were better predictors of women's spatial learning abilities.

limitations: The active/passive dichotomy is too coarse, as 'active' learning encompasses multiple confounded components.
Desktop VR setups often fail to provide appropriate idiothetic information, making it an inadequate paradigm for testing certain aspects of active learning.
Difficulty in isolating and testing specific active/passive components due to experimental design challenges.
Challenges in equating environment size, visibility, and visual input between active and passive conditions.
The spatial-learning literature has primarily focused on metric survey knowledge, neglecting weaker forms of spatial knowledge (route, ordinal, topological).
Many working memory studies rely on spatial descriptions as stimuli, which may not generalize to immersive spatial learning.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: The paper extends understanding of how idiothetic information, processed through path integration, contributes to different forms of spatial knowledge, particularly metric survey knowledge, in active versus passive learning contexts.

The paper proposes a framework for understanding the distinct and interactive contributions of active (self-motion) and passive (sensory input without self-motion) information to the acquisition of various types of spatial knowledge.

mechanism_chain.description: The causal mechanism describes how idiothetic information, generated during active movement, is processed to form metric survey knowledge.
